Abstract 19

The geological history of the Amazon River is a complex story driven by geodynamic 20

processes operating in the South American plate. In spite of recent research, the pre- 21

Neogene structure of Amazon paleodrainage is still underconstrained. A recent study 22

cratonic in origin during the Cretaceous. However, the extent and duration of this 24

system are not well-constrained. To add new constraints, we investigated the 25

the basin (MD234 and MD238) are dominated by zircon ages between 0.9-1.3 Ga 34

(Grenville/ Sunsás, 30% - 43%) and 0.5-0.7 Ga (Brazilian/Pampean, 26% - 16%) with 35

felsic provenance. The oldest MD234 sample also shows a dominant contribution 36

from Paleozoic zircon (20%). On the other hand, the samples from the southern part 37

of the Madre de Dios Basin (samples MD-2019-4A; MD-2019-10; MD-2019-13; MD- 38

2019-11D and MD-2019-12A) have U-Pb age distributions dominated by zircon ages 39

between 0.9-1.3 Ga (Grenville/Sunsás, 30% - 45%) and 1.54-1.3 Ga (Rondonia-San 40

Ignácio, 16% - 43%), pointing to a cratonic origin for these sedimentary rocks. To 41

elucidate the distinction in provenance between the samples from the northern and 42

southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin, we suggest that a structural barrier (the 43

Madidi Arch (?)) was active during the late Cretaceous. In this scenario, the northern 44

part of the Madre de Dios Basin had similar sedimentary sources as the nearby 45

basins like Huallaga, Bagua, Ucayali, and Marañón, whereas, in the southern part of 46

the basin, sedimentation was influenced by local sources. Together with previously 47

developed between the Cenomanian and Maastrichtian in response to the Purus 49

1. Introduction 54

In terms of global mass transfer from continents to oceans, the Amazon River 55

is the most important river contributor, supplying about 20% of the water (Callède et 56

al., 2004), ~10% of the dissolved load (Gaillardet et al., 2003), and ~3% of the 57

suspended load (Milliman & Syvitski, 1992) to the world’s oceans. According to 58

Filizola & Guyot, (2004), Andean tributaries supply more than 95% of the median 59

annual suspended sediment flux that the Amazon delivers, with 2/3 and 1/3 from the 60

Solimões and Madeira rivers, respectively. Its basin drainage includes several Meso- 61

Cenozoic basins located between the Andes and the Atlantic Ocean (Fig. 1). The 62

geological history of the Amazon River and its paleodrainage is complex and its 63

Neogene configuration is a much-discussed subject (Albert et al., 2018; Hoorn et al., 64

2010; Carina Hoorn et al., 2017; Louterbach et al., 2018; Roddaz et al., 2005, 2010; 65

van Soelen et al., 2017a). The majority of previous research has concentrated on two 66

aspects concerning the Amazon River: the precise moment of its 67

transcontinentalization (Figueiredo et al., 2009; Gorini et al., 2014; Hoorn et al., 2017; 68

van Soelen et al., 2017b) and the  geodynamic systems, such as Andean uplift, flat- 69

slab subduction or dynamic topography, that potentially drove this (Eakin et al., 2014; 70

Rodríguez Tribaldos et al., 2017; Sacek, 2014; Shephard et al., 2010). In spite of 71


<!-- Page 5 -->


new researches (e.g. Hurtado et al., 2018; Rodríguez Tribaldos et al., 2017; Stewart 72

et al., 2016), the Amazon basin’s pre-Neogene arrangement has garnered 73

considerably less focus. 74

Recent studies on sedimentary rocks from the Peruvian and Ecuadorian retro 75

arc foreland basins have shown major changes in the drainage system of the 76

western Amazon between the Albian and the early Paleocene (Erlich et al., 2018; 77

George et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Hurtado et al., 2018; et al., 2018). Based 78

on the ɛNd values (between – 16.8 to -18.6) and the detrital zircon grain, which were 79

originated from the easternmost Brazilian Shield terranes Hurtado et al. (2018) 80

suggested the existence of a long-lived cratonic drainage system originated from the 81

Purus Arch (Fig. 1) in the Central-Eastern part of the Brazilian Shield during the 82

Albian-Maastrichtian (from ca 110 Ma to 66 Ma). This cratonic drainage system may 83

be considered the western part of the Cretaceous continent-wide cratonic drainage of 84

the northern part of South America termed “Sanozama” paleodrainage (Almeida, 85

1974; Potter, 1997). However, the study of Hurtado et al. (2018) is based on two 86

Cretaceous samples from the Huallaga Basin and one from the northern part of the 87

Madre de Dios Basin. Hence, the extent and duration of this continent-wide cratonic 88

drainage system during the Cretaceous and how it detected other western 89

Amazonian basins is far from being constrained. 90

In this study, we refine the extent and duration of the long-lived cratonic 91

drainage system in Western Amazonia based on the provenance study of 92

Cretaceous sedimentary rocks deposited in the Acre and Madre de Dios basins. We 93

present whole-rock geochemistry, Sm-Nd isotopic composition, and U-Pb zircon 94

ages to understand the regional configuration and evolution of western Amazonian 95

basins. Through compilations with recent studies, our data indicate that the long-lived 96


<!-- Page 6 -->


paleodrainage system developed between the Cenomanian and Maastrichtian and 97

reached its maximum paleogeographic extension in the Maastrichtian in response to 98

the Purus Arch uplift. 99

2. Geological settings and sampling 101

2.1. Cretaceous stratigraphy of western Amazonian basins 102

The Cretaceous paleogeography of northern South America was strongly 103

controlled by the geodynamic process related to Gondwana’s breakup and the 104

convergence between the Nazca and South America plates (Zamora & Gil, 2018). 105

Since Cretaceous times western Amazonia (Fig.1) sedimentary basins, such as the 106

Oriente/Marañón, Santiago, Bagua, Ucayali, Huallaga, Madre de Dios, and Acre 107

basins experienced a complex structural evolution (Baby et al., 2005; Erlich et al., 108

2018; George et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Hermoza et al., 2006; Louterbach et 109

al., 2018; Martinez et al., 1999; Roddaz et al., 2005; Wine et al., 2001; Zamora & Gil, 110

2018) (Figs. 1 and 2). These basins are presently divided into two parts, the northern 111

and the southern Amazonian retroarc foreland basin (N. Espurt et al., 2007; Roddaz 112

et al., 2005b), because of the uplift of the Fitzcarrald Arch in the Pliocene (Espurt et 113

al., 2007); ( Espurt et al., 2010; Roddaz et al., 2010). 114

The Oriente Basin is made up of Paleozoic to Quaternary sedimentary rocks 115

and sediments (Christophoul et al., 2002). Prolonged to the north by the Putumayo 116

Basin of Colombia and to the south by the Marañón Basin (Fig. 1), the Oriente Basin 117

displays three stratigraphic units ranging in age from the Carboniferous to the Recent 118

(Baby et al., 1999). The first Cretaceous sequence is formed by the Hollin and Napo 119

Formations, which is composed of sandstones, limestones, and organic-rich shales 120

(Fig. 2). The Albian sandstones from the Hollin Formation were deposited above the 121


<!-- Page 7 -->


pre-Albian unconformity (Baby et al., 2013) and derived from the Amazon craton 122

(Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Ruiz et al., 2007). The Upper Cretaceous Napo Formation 123

sedimentary rocks are derived from eastern cratonic sources, mainly from the 124

Rondonian-San Ignacio terrane (1.8 – 1.3 Ga) (Gutiérrez et al., 2019). The Tena 125

Formation (Maastrichtian-Paleocene) exhibits fine-grained reddish sediments that 126

were deposited in a fluvial setting within a distal foredeep deposition zone (Baby et 127

al., 2013). The sedimentary sources were related to the exhumation of the Cordillera 128

Real to the west (Ruiz et al., 2004) and the recycling of ancient formations (Hollin 129

and Napo formations) (Gutiérrez et al., 2019). 130

The Cretaceous sequences of the Oriente Basin are correlated to those of the 131

Marañón Basin (Zamora & Gil, 2018), which is located southward between the 132

Ucayali and Acre basins (Fig. 1). The Cretaceous sedimentary succession within the 133

Marañón Basin begins with the deposition of the sandstones of the Cushabatay 134

Formation in a fluvial to shoreface environments as a product from the Jurua orogeny 135

reactivation (Caputo, 2014; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The Cretaceous sedimentary rocks 136

were deposited after an erosional hiatus (110-120 Ma) and are the calcareous green 137

shales, interbedded with sandstones and platform limestones of the Raya Formation 138

(equivalent to the Napo Basal in the Oriente Basin; Fig. 2) (Zamora and Gil, 2018). 139

The Albian to early Cenomanian Agua Caliente Formation is characterized by 140

sandstones and shales deposited into fluvial-deltaic and marine settings (Zamora & 141

Gil, 2018) The transition between this formation and the Chonta Formation is 142

progressive (Wine et al., 2001; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The Chonta Formation is 143

composed of sandstones, limestones, and shales and consists of the source rock of 144

the Oriente - Marañón prolific oil province (Calderon et al., 2017). This unit defines 145

three transgressive-regressive sequences (Zamora and Gil, 2018). During the 146


<!-- Page 8 -->


Turonian, limestones and black shales were deposited. From the Coniacian to 147

Santonian marine shales interbedded with sandstones and limestones were 148

deposited. The contact between the Chonta Formation and the middle Campanian - 149

late Maastrichtian, fluvial to shallow marine Vivian Formation is erosive (Calderon et 150

al., 2017; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The late Maastrichtian Vivian-Cachiyacu formations 151

represent the last Cretaceous deposition cycle and were formed by sandstones, 152

shales, and limestones (Calderon et al., 2017) (Fig. 2). 153

The Ucayali Basin is limited from the Marañón Basin by the NW-SE Contaya 154

Arch and from the Acre Basin, by the NNW-SSE Moa Divisor structure (Fig. 1). The 155

sedimentary thickness of the basin decreases progressively to the south and towards 156

the Fitzcarrald Arch (Hermoza et al., 2006; Lopez-Gamundi & Lopez-Gamundi, 157

2018). The Cretaceous sedimentation started with the Cushabatay and Raya 158

formations during the Neocomian – Aptian (Martinez et al., 1999). They consist of 159

fluvial to marginal clastics and marine limestones, which progressively disappear to 160

the NNE/SSW (Fig. 2) (Martinez et al., 1999). The Chonta Formation is made up of 161

shales and limestones (Calderon et al., 2017). The end of the Cretaceous is 162

represented by the Maastrichtian quartz-rich sandstones of the Vivian Formation 163

(Martinez et al., 1999). 164

The Huallaga Basin is bounded by the Eastern Cordillera to the west and the 165

Chazuta thrust-related anticline to the east (Hurtado et al., 2018). An erosional 166

unconformity separates the Cretaceous sedimentary succession which is made up 167

from the bottom to the top, by the Cushabatay, Raya, Agua Caliente, Chonta, 168

Cashiyacu, and Vivian formations. The Cushabatay Formation consists of quartz-rich 169

sandstones interbedded with shales and siltstones and deposited by fluvial-deltaic 170

systems during Aptian-Albian times (Hurtado et al., 2018; Wine et al., 2001). The 171


<!-- Page 9 -->


middle-late Albian Raya Formation was deposited in a shallow marine environment 172

and consists of shales, siltstones, and sparse calcareous beds (Hurtado et al., 2018; 173

Sanchez et al., 1997). The Cenomanian Agua Caliente deposits are composed of 174

fluvial-deltaic sandstones interbedded with shales and siltstones (Sanchez et al., 175

1997). The Coniacian-Turonian Chonta Formation is composed of marine shales, 176

marls, mudstones, and limestones (Hurtado et al., 2018). This stratigraphic pile ends 177

in the Maastrichtian with the fluvial coastal quartz-rich sandstones of the Vivian 178

Formation whose marine equivalent is the Cachiyacu Formation (Hurtado et al., 179

2018; Sanchez et al., 1997). 180

The southern Peruvian Madre de Dios Basin is limited to the southwest by the 181

Azulmayo thrust, to the north and northeast by the Brazilian Shield, and to the north- 182

northwest by the Fitzcarrald Arch ( Louterbach et al., 2018). The basement of the 183

basin includes Precambrian to Cambrian metamorphic rocks, Paleozoic 184

metasediments, and tardi-Hercynian igneous rocks ( Louterbach et al., 2018). To the 185

east at the boundary with the Eastern Cordillera, the Madre de Dios Basin 186

encompasses a heterogeneous sedimentary succession of sedimentary rocks 187

deposited between the Upper Paleozoic and the Cenozoic ( Louterbach et al., 2018). 188

The deposits from the early Cretaceous did not undergo preservation, while the 189

sedimentary succession of the late Cretaceous began above a basal regional 190

unconformity (Louterbach, 2014). It is then followed by estuarine sandstones from 191

the Basal Chonta Formation followed by littoral to intertidal gray carbonaceous 192

shales, mudstones siltstones, and sandstones from the Cenomanian-Turonian 193

Chonta Formation (Louterbach, 2014). The Vivian Formation started with red shales 194

and paleosol horizons formed during the late Campanian in a fluvial-tidal coastal 195

plain (Louterbach et al., 2018). The late Maastrichtian Vivian Formation is 196


<!-- Page 10 -->


characterized by sandstones, deposited in a coastal environment with continental 197

inputs (Louterbach, 2014; Louterbach et al., 2018). 198

The Acre Basin is limited to the east and north by the Iquitos Arch, to the 199

northwest by the Marañón Basin, to the west by the Ucayali Basin, and to the south 200

by the Madre de Dios Basin (Cunha, 2007; Haag, 2019). According to (Oliveira, 201

1994), this basin was affected by complex compressional and extensional events 202

from the Paleozoic to the Present. The Albian-Cenomanian sandstones from the 203

lower Moa Formation were followed by transgressive Cenomanian/Turonian black 204

shales of the upper part of this unit. During the Turonian-Campanian, black shales 205

and fine-grained sandstones of the Rio Azul Formation were deposited. The late 206

Campanian Divisor Formation was made up of fluvial sandstones (Cunha, 2007). 207

The sedimentary units from the late Cretaceous of the Marañón, Ucayali, 208

Huallaga, Madre de Dios, and Acre basins may be correlated with the Alter do Chão 209

Formation from the Solimões and Amazonia basins (Caputo, 2014; Hurtado et al., 210

2018). The Jurassic Envira Arch separates the Acre from the Solimões Basin and the 211

Purus Arch limited the Solimões and Amazonas basins (Caputo, 2014) (Fig. 1). The 212

Purus Arch formed as a result of Neoproterozoic compressive stress that caused the 213

inversion of the Cachimbo Graben (Caputo & Soares, 2016; Wanderley Filho et al., 214

2007). The Purus Arch experienced episodes of uplift and subsidence after the 215

Pennsylvanian (Caputo & Soares, 2016; Wanderley Filho et al., 2007). Because of 216

the presence of the Cenozoic deposits and the absence of the Cretaceous 217

sedimentary rocks around the Purus Arch (Caputo & Soares, 2016), the Purus Arch 218

could be topographically high during the Cretaceous as Hurtado et al. (2018) 219

suggested. 220

2.2. Potential sources 222

Detrital zircon U-Pb ages have been used in provenance studies in the Andes- 223

Amazonian basins to interpret the possible contributions of Cratonic and Andean 224

source rocks during the sedimentary evolution (Chavez et al., 2022; Erlich et al., 225

2018; George et al., 2019; Horton et al., 2015; Horton, 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018; 226

Louterbach et al., 2018; Moreno et al., 2020; Nie et al., 2012). The relative sources 227

have different types of terranes and different ages. Precambrian zircon U-Pb ages 228

(>900 Ma) are found in the Amazon craton which is a continental block resulting from 229

lateral crustal accretionary processes that lasted from Archean to Mesoproterozoic 230

(Cordani & Teixeira, 2007; Santos et al., 2000; Tassinari & Macambira, 1999). 231

Neoproterozoic and Phanerozoic zircon U-Pb ages (<900 Ma) could be related to 232

rocks from the fold and thrust belts formed during the amalgamation of the 233

Supercontinent Gondwana. These rocks were affected by the Brazilian Event (Brito 234

Neves, 2002), and by magmatic events on western Gondwana related to a polycyclic 235

orogenic history ( Chew et al., 2008; Chew et al., 2007; Chew et al., 2016) (Fig. 3). 236

Nd isotopes may be used as a provenance tool because they are not easily 237

fractionated by sedimentary or post-depositional processes (Konieczna et al., 2015; 238

Mahoney, 2005; McLennan et al., 1990). Cratonic-derived river sediments have 239

εNd(0) values between -14.5 and -20, while Andean-derived sediments have εNd(0) 240

values >-13.8 (Figueiredo et al., 2009; Horbe et al., 2013; Roddaz et al., 2005). This 241

difference in the Nd isotopes recorded in fine-grained sediments has been used to 242

decipher the provenance and reconstruct the paleodrainage systems in Western 243

Amazonia (e. g. Roddaz et al., 2005; Louterbach et al., 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018). 244

2.3. Sampling and stratigraphic constraints 245

3. Materials and methods 313

3.1. Major and trace element concentrations 314

The major and trace element concentrations were measured at the Service 315

d’Analyse des Roches et Mineraux (SARM, INSU facility, Vandoeuvre-Les-Nancy, 316

France) by ICP-OES and ICP-MS. Analytical details are available on 317

http://helium.crpg.cnrs-nancy.fr/SARM/ and in (Carignan et al., 2001). Precision is 318

better than 5% for elements measured by ICP-OES, and 10% for elements measured 319

by ICP-MS (see supplementary dataset for details). 320

3.2. Sm-Nd isotope composition 321

The Sm-Nd isotope composition of the analyzed was made at the Geochronos 322

Laboratory of the Geosciences Institute, Universidade de Brasília, following the 323

methods described by Goia & Pimentel (2000). The isotopic ratios of Sm and Nd 324

were measured using a Thermo Scientific TRITON Plus thermal ionization mass 325

spectrometer. The precision of the measurements was estimated by analyzing the 326

BHVO-2 standard and repeated analysis gave a 143Nd/144Nd ratio of 0.512996 ± 327

0.000006 (2SD, n=10) (Weis et al., 2005). 328

The measured 143Nd/144Ndsample and 143Sm/144Ndsample ratios were expressed in ɛ 329

notation and reflect the fractional deviation in parts per 104 unit from the 143Sm/144Nd 330

from the Chondritic Uniform Reservoir (CHUR) as described by Jacobsen & 331

Wasserburg (1980). The TDM and TDM* ages were calculated following (Augustsson 332

& Bahlburg, 2008; DePaolo et al., 1991; DePaolo, 1981; Albarède & Brouxel, 1987 333

and Goldstein et al., 1984) as demonstrated in the supplementary dataset. 334

5. Discussion 477

5.1. Influence of geochemical characteristics in the provenance sedimentary 478

interpretation. 479

The utilization of elemental ratios (Cr/Th, Th/Sc, Zr/Sc), Eu anomalies 480

(Eu/Eu*) and Sm-Nd isotopic compositions of sedimentary rock have proven to be 481

valuable in determining the source of ancient sediments (McLennan et al., 1993). 482

However, it is essential to consider the potential effects of grain-size sorting and 483

diagenesis on trace element ratios, REE concentration, and radiogenic isotope 484

composition of the analyzed sedimentary rocks. 485

Except for the samples AC 33 (0.42) and AC 27A (0.44), most of the Acre 486

Basin samples have a low Al/Si ratio (0.01 - 0.27) (Fig. 6), which indicates that they 487

are enriched in quartz. However, the lack of Al/Si with REE content, Eu/Eu*, Cr/Th, 488

and ƐNd (0) correlation (seen in the supplementary dataset) suggests sedimentary 489

sorting has not made any alteration of these provenance indicators. Nevertheless, 490

the REE concentrations of the analyzed samples against PAAS show contrasting 491


<!-- Page 22 -->


patterns. Only one sample of the Acre Basin (Sample AC 38) plots in the shale field 492

(Fig. 9) whereas the remaining ten samples plot outside of the shale field suggesting 493

that the REE concentrations have been perturbed by post-depositional processes 494

(Fig. 9). The AC 22A show strong enrichment in HREE (Fig. 9). This strong HREE 495

enrichment could be associated with a primary phase of the pedologic process. In a 496

study of the lateritic process in a tropical environment, Viers and Wasserburg (2004) 497

indicated that the zircon dissolution could elevate the HREE concentrations at the 498

early stage of the weathering process, and the Zr precipitation could remove the REE 499

during that phase. This could explain the HREE enrichment for samples AC 22, 27A, 500

and 38. The remaining samples (AC 15A, 42B, 30A, 20A2, 37, and 49) show 501

enrichment in LREE over HREE and plot between the “shales” and “seawater” fields 502

in Fig. 9. 503

The Madre de Dios samples have a high Al/Si ratio which ranges between 504

0.33 and 0.44 (except for MD-2019-11E, Al/Si = 0.23), which suggests that are fine 505

and clay-rich sediments (Bouchez et al., 2011) (Table 3, Fig. 9). The lack of 506

correlation (see in the supplementary dataset) between CIA and Al/Si with REE 507

content, Eu/Eu*, Cr/Th, and ƐNd (0) values implies that the provenance indicators 508

have not been altered by chemical weathering and sedimentary sorting. The samples 509

exhibit low Eu/Eu* ratios (Table 3) indicating that diagenetic remobilization of Eu was 510

insignificant in our samples. The Madre de Dios samples have more uniform major 511

and trace elements and REE concentration patterns when compared with those of 512

the Acre Basin (Figs. 5A and 5B). The analyzed samples from Madre de Dios exhibit 513

Ce anomalies (ΩCe) above 0.85 and display flat REE patterns when compared to 514

PAAS, indicating their classification within “shales” field (Fig. 9). This characteristic, 515


<!-- Page 23 -->


typical of continental clays (see Moiroud et al., (2016), suggest that these samples 516

are unaffected  by marine autogenesis. 517

5.2. Interpretation of provenance 518

The Th/Sc, Cr/Th elemental ratios and the Eu/Eu* ratios of the Acre Basin 519

samples are in favor of a silicic/felsic source sensu Cullers (2000) source: the Th/Sc 520

is between 0. and 4.5; the Cr/Th ratios are equal or higher than 1.0 and the Eu/Eu* 521

ratios are between 0.50 - 0.65. This is also the case for the analyzed Madre de Dios 522

sedimentary rocks with Th/Sc ratio range (0.64 - 0.87); Cr/Th ratio (between 5.14 and 523

7.23), and Eu/Eu* values (0.59 and 0.67 (Table 3, Fig. 8) characteristics of 524

silicic/felsic sources (Cullers, 2000). Further insights can be obtained by considering 525

the Nd isotopic composition of the analyzed samples, which can provide additional 526

constrains. 527

Therefore, the Nd isotopic compositions observed in sedimentary rocks from 528

the Andean and Amazonian regions can be attributed to a combination between 529

juvenile primitive Andean Arc and older cratonic sources (Basu et al., 1990; Roddaz 530

et al., 2005). Cratonic sedimentary rocks are characterized by negative ƐNd (0) 531

values, between -14.5 and -20, and Nd model ages (TDM) from 1.75 to 3.3 Ga, while 532

Andean-derived sediments have more positive ƐNd (0) values and TDM lower than 1.6 533

Ga (Cordani & Sato, 1999; Figueiredo et al., 2009; Carina Hoorn et al., 2017; Horbe 534

et al., 2013; Roddaz et al., 2005). Within Colombia, a threshold value of -12.7 for 535

εNd(0) has been employed to differentiate sedimentary rocks derived from the 536

Andean or cratonic sources  (Nie et al., 2012). Similarly, zircon U-Pb ages have been 537

used in provenance studies of Amazonian sediments to decipher the relative 538

contributions of Andean and cratonic source rocks (Erlich et al., 2018; George et al., 539

2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Horton, 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018; Louterbach et al., 540


<!-- Page 24 -->


2018; Moreno et al., 2020; Perez et al., 2016). The distinct geological ages of the 541

Andean Cordillera and the Amazon craton account for their compositional 542

differences. For instance, the Amazon craton is defined by Precambrian zircon U–Pb 543

ages (>600 Ma, Fig. 3) (Bahlburg et al., 2009; Chew et al., 2008; Chew et al., 2007; 544

Cordani et al., 2000; Cordani & Sato, 1999; Rizzotto & Quadros, 2005; Santos et al., 545

2000; Tassinari & Macambira, 1999). In contrast, the Andes are mostly characterized 546

by Phanerozoic zircon U-Pb ages (<550 Ma, mainly Mesozoic-Cenozoic ages, Fig. 3) 547

(DeCelles et al., 2011; Horton et al., 2016; Martin-Gombojav & Winkler, 2008; Nie et 548

al., 2012; Perez et al., 2016), except for the Marañón Complex which crops out in the 549

Peruvian Eastern Cordillera. The Marañón complex is composed of metamorphic and 550

plutonic rocks of the Precambrian age (Chew et al., 2007; Ramos & Folguera, 2009). 551

Except for the three youngest samples of the Campanian-Maastrichtian 552

Divisor Formation (AC 20 A2, AC 16, and AC 15A) that could have been perturbed 553

5.3. Implications for the paleogeographic evolution of Cretaceous Andes- 651

Amazonian drainage 652

Our results suggest different sedimentary provenances for the Cenomanian- 653

Maastrichtian samples of the Acre Basin, the late Cretaceous samples of the 654

northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin, and the Cenomanian-Maastrichtian 655

samples of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin. We suggest that these 656

distinct source areas reflect different paleodrainage networks. Our provenance 657

results also bring new time constraints on the Cretaceous continent-wide cratonic 658

paleodrainage of the northern part of South America termed “Sanozama” 659

paleodrainage (Almeida, 1974; Potter, 1997) and on its geographic extension in 660

Western Amazonia. We thus propose the following scenario: 1) during the Albian- 661

Cenomanian, Western Amazonia is fragmented into several sub-basins fed by local 662

sources; 2) during the Cenomanian-Campanian, the provenance of western 663

Amazonian basins located north of the Ucayali Basin (Fig. 1) is dominated by input 664


<!-- Page 29 -->


from Ventuari-Tapajos terranes likely sourced by the incipient uplift of the Purus 665

Arch; the incipient cratonic drainage is estimated to be Cenomanian in age; 3) In the 666

early Maastrichtian, this drainage reached its acme and sourced the northern part of 667

the Madre de Dios Basin but not the southern part that was probably isolated from 668

the northern part by the Madidi Arch (Fig. 11). 669

Based on our data, it is evident that the source of the late Cretaceous 670

sedimentary rocks in both the northern and southern regions of the Madre de Dios 671

Basin exhibits distinct variations (Figs. 7 and 8). This difference in provenance may 672

imply the existence of a topographic barrier separating the paleodrainage systems of 673

act as a topographic barrier during the late Cretaceous: the Manu and Madidi arches 676

(House et al., 1999). The Paleozoic series of both arches have been completely 677

eroded, exposing crystalline basement rocks along their axes during the late Permian 678

to the late Cretaceous period. The Manu Arch is an NW-SE structure that separates 679

the Ucayali Basin from the Madre de Dios Basin (Fig. 1) and hence due to its 680

geographical location, it cannot explain the difference in provenance within the 681

sedimentary rocks of the Madre de Dios Basin. The Madidi Arch is trending 682

westwards from northern Bolivia towards the Sub-Andean Zone (SAZ) in 683

southeastern Peru (House et al., 1999) (Fig. 1). Although its geographical position 684

needs to be better constrained in the SAZ, recent reconstruction suggests that it may 685

separate the analyzed sedimentary rocks of the southern part from those of the 686

northern part (see Fig. 16 in ( Baby et al., 2018). Thus, we consider the uplift of 687

Madidi Arch may be the best candidate for a topographic barrier capable of 688

separating the paleodrainage of the northern and southern parts of the Madre de 689

Dios Basin. However, other hypotheses cannot be highlighted, such as SW Amazon 690

Craton uplift (?) or stratigraphic sequence changes (?). Given that the mechanisms 691

(rift shoulder (?), intracratonic deformation? forebulge uplift?) at the origin of the 692

Cretaceous uplift of the Madidi Arch are unknown, more work is needed to resolve 693

this issue. 694

15) we argue that the change of the dominant sedimentary input occurred during the 711

dominated by Rio Negro – Juruena (1.54 – 1.82 Ga) and Ventuari Tapajos (1.82-2.0 713

The difference in provenance between samples from the northern and southern parts 727

of the Madre de Dios Basin and the absence of dominant Ventuari – Tapajos (1.82 – 728

2.0Ga) zircon population in the samples from the southern part of the Madre de Dios 729

drainage reached its acme (widest paleogeographical extension) in the early 732

Maastrichtian. 733

The existence of the continent-wide paleodrainage was controlled by the uplift 734

history of the Central part of the Amazon Craton and the Purus Arch. However, the 735

mechanism(s) at the origin of the Cenomanian-Maastrichtian uplift of the Central part 736

of the Amazon Craton and the Purus Arch remains unclear. The Purus Arch is an 737

elevated area, located 240 km west of Manaus and parallel to NW-SE strike-slip 738

faults (Costa et al., 2001) that separate the Amazonas and Solimões Basins. It 739


<!-- Page 32 -->


consists of a regional structure that originated from distension during the 740

Mesoproterozoic Era (Caputo and Soares, 2016 and references therein). The Purus 741

Arch was likely exposed from the Neoproterozoic until the Early of the Pennsylvanian 742

and probably experienced uplift and erosion during the Cretaceous because 743

Cretaceous sedimentary rocks are absent in the region of the Purus Arch (Caputo 744

and Soares, 2016). This may suggest that the Purus Arch was an important 745

paleogeographic barrier during the late Cretaceous. 746

Different investigations have recorded an elevation of the eastern sectors of 747

the Central Brazilian and Guyana shields during the late Cretaceous (Caputo & 748

Soares, 2016; Harman et al., 1998; Hurtado et al., 2018; Potter, 1997; Roddaz et al., 749

2021; Vallejo et al., 2017).The estimation of denudations rates using apatite fission 750

track analysis during the late Cretaceous in the Central Brazilian Shield led to the 751

interpretation that an important phase of tectonic reactivation occurred in the region 752

between the early Campanian and late Maastrichtian (~80 to 60 Ma) (Harman et al., 753

1998). The elevation and erosion of the Central Brazilian shield were facilitated by 754

the emergence of the Brazilian Carajás region in the northeastern Amazon region 755

around 80 Ma (Monteiro et al., 2018). Furthermore, a similar mechanism was 756

proposed for the central part of the Guiana Shield during the Campanian (Sapin et 757

al., 2016). The uplifted surface likely influenced the paleodrainage evolution of this 758

region after the Coniacian (~86 Ma) (Roddaz et al., 2021). Drainage reorganizations 759

during the late Cretaceous are also identified in the cost line of NW Africa, 760

characterized by an increased influx of Precambrian sediments during the 761

Campanian – Maastrichtian, related to the opening of the South and Equatorial 762

Atlantic Ocean (Mourlot et al., 2018). Similar geodynamic system may be occurred in 763

the northeastern and northwestern South America and West African cratons during 764


<!-- Page 33 -->


the opening of the Aquatorial Ocean, leading to surface uplift. This elevation of the 765

Atlantic margins in the late Cretaceous can be explained by intracontinental 766

deformation resulting from significant changes in plate motions between Africa, 767

Antartica, and South America (see Harman et al., 1998 and references therein), as 768

well as mantle upwelling beneath the margin (Matton and Jébrak, 2009). These 769

processes may have contributed to the late Cretaceous uplift of the Purus Arch and 770

the Central part of the Amazon Craton, potentially influencing the paleodrainage 771

evolution of Western Amazonia during the Cenomanian-Maastrichtian. 772

6. Conclusions 774

The analysis based on a multi-proxy dataset, including major and trace elements 775

concentrations, Sm-Nd isotopic composition, and detrital zircon U-Pb ages, used to 776

identify the sources of Cretaceous sedimentary rocks from the Acre and Madre de 777

Dios basins (Brazil and Peru) results in the following conclusions: 778

• The Cretaceous sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the Madre de Dios 779

Basin have different provenances. The oldest late Cretaceous sedimentary rocks 780

(MD234 and MD238) are sourced by mixed Andean (Eastern Cordillera)-Cratonic 781

sources whereas the early Maastrichtian sedimentary rock (MD239) analyzed in 782

Louterbach et al. (2018) was sourced by the Central Brazilian Shield; 783

• The Cenomanian – Maastrichtian samples from the southern part of the Madre 784

de Dios Basin have similar Andean provenance as the late Maastrichtian sample 785

(MD176) of the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin analyzed in Louterbach et 786

al. (2018). They did not share the same provenance as those of the northern part 787

suggesting that a topographic barrier (the Madidi Arch (?)) might have separated the 788

northern part from the southern part during the late Cretaceous; 789


<!-- Page 34 -->


• The Cenomanian-Maastrichtian sedimentary rocks of the Acre Basin have εNd 790

(0) values consistent with a Cratonic source with silicic contribution and U-Pb zircon 791

age distribution dominated by Amazon Craton zircon grains (Ventuari-Tapajos (2.0- 792

1.8 Ga) and Rio Negro-Juruena (1.8-1.54 Ga)) sourced by the continent-wide 793

drainage system. These data suggest that the cratonic drainage system was initiated 794

younger than previously thought, probably in response to the uplift of the Purus Arch 795

ascribed to geodynamic process (intracontinental deformation or mantle upwelling) 796

during the opening of the Atlantic Equatorial Ocean. 797

Our provenance data also suggest that the continent-wide cratonic drainage 798

reached its maximum paleogeographic extension during the early Maastrichtian and 799

was the main source of sediments for the Ecuadorian, Peruvian, and Brazilian 800

western Amazonia Basins. Contrary to the Cenozoic period, the influence of the 801

Andes on Western Amazonia paleogeography was minor during the Cenomanian- 802

early Maastrichtian. 803
